subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Synthetic Fuels
description: A short lesson to help you apply Synthetic Fuels.

hook.text: What if you could make gasoline from thin air—literally combining captured CO2 with green hydrogen?

buildup.text: Synthetic fuels, or e-fuels, do exactly that—creating liquid hydrocarbons that work in existing engines.

discovery.text: Porsche invested in a plant in Chile that makes e-fuel using wind power, water, and atmospheric CO2.

twist.text: E-fuels are carbon-neutral in theory but wildly expensive—about five times the cost of regular gasoline.

climax.text: They may save classic cars and race cars from extinction in an electrified world, even if mass use is unlikely.

punchline.text: Synthetic fuel lets old engines run on new energy—at a steep price.

quiz.question: What are synthetic fuels (e-fuels) made from?

details.summary: Synthetic fuels, or e-fuels, are produced by combining captured CO2 with green hydrogen, creating liquid hydrocarbons that can run in conventional engines with near-zero net carbon emissions.
details.whyItMatters: Synthetic fuels could keep existing combustion engines running cleanly, offering a bridge for vehicles and industries that are difficult to electrify directly.
takeaways: E-fuels combine green hydrogen with captured carbon dioxide
They work in existing engines without modification
Production costs remain several times higher than fossil fuels

faq.question: Can synthetic fuels make gasoline cars carbon neutral?
faq.answer: In theory, yes. If the CO2 used to create the fuel equals the CO2 emitted when burned, the cycle is carbon neutral. In practice, production energy and transport add some emissions.

faq.question: Why doesn't Porsche just make electric cars instead of investing in e-fuels?
faq.answer: Porsche is doing both. E-fuels target the millions of existing combustion cars and motorsport applications where battery weight and charging logistics pose challenges.
